It is confined to the aortic root and pulmonary artery
It involves the left side only, affects the septum and anterior wall, and spares the apex and posterior wall

It is an ARVD variant with desmosome mutation, only in athletes and a dagger sign
It is an RCM variant with amyloid, only in elderly women and low voltage

questions.sec: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology

Microvascular inflammation → normal coronaries → troponin fall
LV dilatation → increased cavity size → reduced LVEDP → reduced LAP
Aortic regurgitation → wide pulse pressure → low DBP → syncope
questions.exp: The vertical chain begins with concentric LVH, smaller cavity, raised LVEDP and raised LA pressure. (Book p337)

questions.sec: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology

questions.exp: The arrow reads increased cardiac output (from 25 → 40%) under atrial stretch/dilatation. (Book p337)

questions.sec: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology

opts: Flash pulmonary edema → renal stenosis; thromboembolism → LV thrombus
Atrial stretch/dilatation → increased cardiac output and AF risk; raised PCWP → pulmonary edema → dyspnea
Wide pulse pressure → Lincoln sign; aortic regurgitation → nocturnal angina
Systemic congestion → JVP/ascites; atrial enlargement → low voltage
questions.exp: The left arm gives atrial stretch/dilatation with increased CO and AF risk; the right arm gives raised PCWP → pulmonary edema → dyspnea. (Book p337)

questions.sec: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology
questions.q: A patient with HCM becomes breathless during tachycardia despite no change in coronary anatomy. Which printed mechanism explains this?
opts: Worsened aortic regurgitation from prolonged diastole
A pleural effusion causing cough-predominant COPD
Fixed cardiac output from aortic stenosis
Tachycardia-related dyspnea on exertion from diastolic dysfunction
questions.exp: The final line under HCM pathophysiology is tachycardia-related dyspnea on exertion. (Book p337)

questions.sec: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology

opts: Atrial stretch raises the risk of atrial fibrillation
One third of patients have dynamic LVOT obstruction
The septum and anterior wall are asymmetrically hypertrophied
Concentric LVH enlarges the cavity and lowers LVEDP
questions.exp: The page says concentric LVH decreases cavity size and raises LVEDP; the other three are printed. (Book p337)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types

Dilatation of LVOT → low-velocity jet → high-pressure zones → valve closure
Concentric fibrosis → small atria → low RVEDP → edema
Projection into LVOT → narrow LVOT width → high-velocity jet → low-pressure zones on either side of the jet
questions.exp: The top of p338 prints that exact sequence. (Book p338)

questions.exp: The line reads systolic motion of the anterior mitral leaflet (SAM) occurs after 2/3rd of systole. (Book p338)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types

questions.exp: The left branch gives mild MR → PSM at apex; the right gives increased LVOT obstruction → ESM at LLSB. (Book p338)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types
questions.q: What gradient is printed beneath the SAM branches?
questions.exp: The section heading reads gradient (30 mmHg). (Book p338)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types
questions.q: Why does that gradient occur, and what does it determine?
opts: It is due to aortic-root dilatation and determines all peripheral signs
It is due to valve calcification and determines coronary calcium only
It is due to subaortic obstruction (subvalvular AS) and determines progression to heart failure (most important) and symptom severity
It is due to renal-artery stenosis and determines flash edema
questions.exp: The gradient section says due to subaortic obstruction (subvalvular AS) and draws a determinant bracket to progression to HF (most important) and severity of symptoms. (Book p338)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types
questions.q: Match the three aortic-stenosis levels printed in the note — 1) Valvular 2) Subvalvular 3) Supravalvular … A) Least common; Williams syndrome B) Occurs in HCM C) Most common
questions.exp: The note reads valvular (m/c), subvalvular in HCM and supravalvular (Williams syndrome) least common. (Book p338)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types

questions.exp: The gradient bracket marks progression to heart failure as most important, along with symptom severity. (Book p338)

questions.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types

SAM occurs before one third of systole
The anterior mitral leaflet is drawn into the septum/LVOT

questions.sec: HCM Symptoms, Pulse and Apex Signs, Heart Sounds, Murmurs and the Principle of Dynamic Auscultation

Hypertensive crisis and cannon waves; pulsus alternans; P = T
Narrow pulse pressure and raised JVP; pulsus tardus; no bisferiens
Wide BP and raised JVP; collapsing pulse; P < T; third peak from AI
questions.exp: The signs read BP normal, JVP normal, jerky pulse and pulsus bisferiens with its two peaks and SAM relation. (Book p339)

questions.sec: HCM Symptoms, Pulse and Apex Signs, Heart Sounds, Murmurs and the Principle of Dynamic Auscultation

questions.sec: HCM Symptoms, Pulse and Apex Signs, Heart Sounds, Murmurs and the Principle of Dynamic Auscultation

questions.exp: The four lines read S1 normal, S2 reverse split, S3 + and S4 ++ with those explanations. (Book p339)

ESM at LLSB and PSM at apex; intensity varies with the LV–aorta pressure gradient, whose factors are preload, afterload and inotropy

EDM at base and MDM at apex; factors are heart rate, temperature and hemoglobin

questions.exp: Wide pulse pressure/collapsing pulse is an AR sign; HCM has normal BP/JVP and bisferiens. (Book p339)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: Match the preferred loading state for HCM — 1) Preload 2) Afterload 3) Inotropy … A) Low B) High C) High
questions.exp: The top row reads high preload, high afterload and low inotropy. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: Which three harmful mechanisms are drawn beneath the loading states?
opts: High preload stretches the pericardium; high afterload closes the aortic valve; low inotropy causes SAM

Low preload reduces cavity size and raises obstruction/gradient/severity; reduced afterload leaves less blood in the LV and narrows the LVOT; increased inotropy draws the septum and mitral valve into the LVOT
Low preload causes wide pulse pressure; low afterload causes cyanosis; high inotropy causes pleural effusion
All three lower LVEDP and abolish the gradient
questions.exp: Those are the three vertically printed mechanism chains under preload, afterload and inotropy. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: Match each relieving or aggravating factor — 1) Relieving 2) Preload aggravators 3) Afterload aggravator 4) Inotropy aggravators … A) Hydration (raised preload) B) Aggressive fall in BP C) Moderate–severe activity and digoxin-type inotropes (contraindicated to elevate BP) D) Venodilators and diuretics
questions.exp: Hydration relieves; venodilators/diuretics lower preload; aggressive BP reduction lowers afterload; moderate–severe activity and inotropes such as digoxin increase inotropy. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: Match each dynamic manoeuvre to the column it occupies — 1) Valsalva while standing 2) Amyl nitrite 3) Isoproterenol 4) Hand grip … A) Decreases murmur intensity by raising afterload B) Increases intensity by lowering preload C) Increases intensity by raising force of contraction D) Increases intensity by lowering afterload
questions.exp: Three manoeuvres sit in the increase-intensity column; hand grip and phenylephrine raise afterload in the decrease-intensity column. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Valsalva note and hand-grip partner.
opts: True — standing Valsalva lowers all other murmurs but increases HCM intensity and MVP duration
False — MVP and HCM are the only murmurs that decrease
True — standing Valsalva increases every murmur equally
questions.exp: The note says all murmurs decrease with standing Valsalva except MVP (increased duration) and HCM (increased intensity); hand grip raises afterload. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: Which second drug shares the decreased-intensity column with hand grip?
questions.exp: The decrease-intensity column lists hand grip and phenylephrine with increased afterload. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG

Complete heart block and atrial standstill
questions.exp: The investigations bullets are LVH and, in precordial leads, ST–T changes/deep giant T inversions (Yamaguchi). (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: A patient with HCM stands and performs Valsalva; the ESM becomes louder. What change in loading is the page using to explain this?
questions.exp: The increase-intensity column labels standing Valsalva as decreased preload. (Book p340)

questions.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one intervention should reduce, not aggravate, the HCM murmur.
questions.exp: Hydration raises preload and is the printed relieving factor; the others aggravate obstruction. (Book p340)

Troponin rise, peripheral enhancement and Dallas criteria
Abnormal Holter study, unexplained syncope and LVH >30 mm

questions.q: Match each LV and atrial measurement to its printed value — 1) Systolic function 2) Dimensions 3) Both atria 4) End-diastolic pressure … A) Massively enlarged B) Normal or rarely reduced C) Almost normal D) Raised, RVEDP > LVEDP

units.title: HCM Epidemiology, Mutations, Pediatric Mimics, Complications, the 15-mm Definition and the Athlete-versus-HCM Table
units.sec: HCM Epidemiology, Mutations, Pediatric Mimics, Complications, the 15-mm Definition and the Athlete-versus-HCM Table
units.guide:
HCM is the most common genetic cardiovascular disease worldwide and the most common cause of SCD; it is autosomal dominant, with myosin binding protein C ranked above myosin heavy chain (p336). Incidence is M = F, females progress more to HF with poor prognosis and 95–99% are asymptomatic.
Paediatric mimics are Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type 2, short PR), Fabry disease, Noonan syndrome and Friedreich ataxia; complications are HF progression, arrhythmias/AF and SCD.
HCM is LV thickness ≥15 mm without dilatation after excluding other capable cardiac/systemic disease; systemic HTN and AS are the other ≥15 mm causes. Athlete's heart has LV thickness <15 mm (10–12 mm), a large cavity, normal diastolic filling and improvement with rest; HCM has ≥15 mm, a small cavity, abnormal filling and no improvement.

units.title: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology
units.sec: Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology
units.guide:
Asymmetric HCM involves only the left side, septal and anterior wall, sparing apex and posterior wall; hypertrophy is inappropriate because afterload is not raised (p337). LVOT obstruction is present in one third, absent/normal in one third and dynamic in one third.
Yamaguchi disease is a Japanese-population HCM variant with apical hypertrophy and deep/giant T inversions. Diastolic dysfunction runs concentric LVH → smaller cavity → raised LVEDP → raised LAP.
Atrial stretch/dilatation raises the atrial CO contribution from 25 to 40% and AF risk; raised PCWP produces pulmonary edema and dyspnea, with tachycardia-related exertional dyspnea.

units.title: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types
units.sec: Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types
units.guide:
Asymmetrical septal hypertrophy projects into the LVOT, narrows it and creates a high-velocity jet with low-pressure zones that draw the anterior mitral leaflet into the septum/LVOT; SAM is printed after two thirds of systole (p338).
Mild secondary MR causes a PSM at the apex, while increased LVOT obstruction causes an ESM at the lower left sternal border. A 30 mmHg gradient reflects subaortic/subvalvular obstruction and determines progression to HF (most important) and symptom severity.
The AS-location note labels valvular most common, subvalvular as the HCM form and supravalvular/Williams least common; angina with normal coronaries is due to microvascular dysfunction.

units.title: HCM Symptoms, Pulse and Apex Signs, Heart Sounds, Murmurs and the Principle of Dynamic Auscultation
units.sec: HCM Symptoms, Pulse and Apex Signs, Heart Sounds, Murmurs and the Principle of Dynamic Auscultation
units.guide:
Again 95–99% are asymptomatic (p339). Raised LAP/LVEDP gives exertional dyspnea/fatigue, orthopnea and PND in advanced disease; LVOT obstruction gives angina/syncope/dyspnea; palpitations come from arrhythmias with AF the commonest sustained arrhythmia, and syncope is repeated separately.
BP and JVP are normal, the pulse is jerky and bisferiens has two systolic peaks with percussion > tidal and the second peak related to SAM obstruction. The double apical impulse is due to SAM and the triple impulse to presystolic accentuation.
S1 is normal, S2 reverse split from prolonged ejection, S3 is + from reduced filling of a non-compliant ventricle and S4 ++ from a vigorously contracting sinus-rhythm atrium. Murmurs are ESM at LLSB and PSM at apex; ESM intensity follows the LV–aorta gradient and preload, afterload and inotropy.

units.title: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
units.sec: Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG
units.guide:
HCM prefers high preload, high afterload and low inotropy (p340). Reduced preload and afterload shrink the cavity/LVOT and raise obstruction; increased inotropy draws septum and mitral valve into the LVOT.
Hydration relieves. Venodilators/diuretics, aggressive BP reduction, moderate–severe activity and inotropes such as digoxin aggravate; inotropes are contraindicated for elevating BP in HCM.
Standing Valsalva, amyl nitrite and isoproterenol increase murmur intensity by lowering preload/afterload or raising contractility; hand grip and phenylephrine reduce it by raising afterload. All murmurs decrease with standing Valsalva except MVP (duration ↑) and HCM (intensity ↑). ECG shows LVH and precordial ST–T changes/deep giant T inversions in Yamaguchi.

units.title: ECHO and the Dagger Sign, Medical Treatment and Beta-Blocker Advantages, CCBs and ICD Indications
units.sec: ECHO and the Dagger Sign, Medical Treatment and Beta-Blocker Advantages, CCBs and ICD Indications
units.guide:
ECHO is the gold standard for HCM and requires ≥15 mm LV thickening without dilatation or another valvular/systemic/cardiac cause; Doppler shows the dagger sign (p341). Medical management is beta blocker or CCB plus disopyramide.
Beta blocker is DOC; propranolol is printed at 2 mg/kg (max 480 mg), reducing exercise HR response and rest/exercise LVOT gradient, relieving angina by lowering myocardial O₂ demand and increasing diastolic filling. CCBs are used for beta-blocker contraindication/intolerance; named drugs are verapamil and diltiazem.
ICD indications are previous cardiac arrest, family history of SCD, sustained VT, abnormal Holter, unexplained syncope and LVH >30 mm.

units.title: Disopyramide, Surgical Management, Restrictive Cardiomyopathy Physiology and Its Clinical Features
units.sec: Disopyramide, Surgical Management, Restrictive Cardiomyopathy Physiology and Its Clinical Features
units.guide:
Disopyramide is class Ia, added to beta blocker/CCB if no relief, with QT prolongation, anticholinergic effects and reduced EF (p342). Surgery is for refractory HCM with gradient >50 mmHg despite medical therapy, by septal myomectomy or alcohol septal ablation.
RCM is introduced as non-genetic, more common than HCM and nested inside diastolic dysfunction. Constrictive pericarditis is the constrictive branch; restrictive physiology and restrictive CMP are the more severe restrictive branch.
RCM ventricles are stiff/non-compliant (R > L), non-dilated and of normal thickness, raising filling pressure and RAP. Systemic congestion gives JVP, ascites, edema and hepatomegaly; atrial stretch raises AF risk. Systolic function is almost normal, dimensions normal/rarely reduced, atria massively enlarged and RVEDP > LVEDP. Subtle exercise intolerance is first, restrictive physiology is the severest diastolic dysfunction and biventricular diastolic failure is R > L.

units.title: RCM Causes and Storage Patterns, the Most Common Mutations, Amyloidosis Classification and Features
units.sec: RCM Causes and Storage Patterns, the Most Common Mutations, Amyloidosis Classification and Features
units.guide:
RCM causes are non-infiltrative DM/scleroderma; intracellular iron (hemochromatosis, dilated > RCM), glycosphingolipid (Fabry) and glycogen (Pompe) accumulation (the latter two HCM > RCM); and intercellular amyloidosis, sarcoidosis (DCM > RCM), Loeffler syndrome and tropical endomyocardial fibrosis (p343). The figure labels lamellar bodies and zebra/onion-skin appearance in Fabry disease, with Ascaris lumbricoides printed as the most common associated infection.
The mutation recap gives DCMP truncated-variant titin, HCM myosin-binding-protein and RCM amyloidosis.
Amyloidosis is classified as primary AL, secondary AA (no heart, only kidney) and familial ATTR, with heart involved in all except secondary AA. ATTR is split into wild senile systemic amyloidosis and mutant familial amyloid polyneuropathy; localized amyloidosis produces atrial natriuretic factor and involves the heart. Features are bilateral thickened ventricles, biatrial dilatation, interatrial septal thickening and diastolic > systolic HF.

units.title: Amyloidosis Investigations, Arrhythmogenic RV Dysplasia, Tachycardia-Induced CMP and Takotsubo Presentation
units.sec: Amyloidosis Investigations, Arrhythmogenic RV Dysplasia, Tachycardia-Induced CMP and Takotsubo Presentation
units.guide:
Amyloidosis ECG shows low-voltage complexes and a pseudo-infarct pattern; ECHO shows hypertrophy (L > R); cardiac MRI shows a glittering hyperrefractile/sparkling myocardium due to interatrial septal thickening, and prognosis is poor (p344).
ARVD is autosomal recessive with mutated desmosomes, fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium and arrhythmias/SCD. Tachycardia-induced CMP follows recurrent tachycardia → myocardial-fibre disruption → CMP → AF.
Takotsubo is also called broken-heart syndrome, transient apical ballooning, neurogenic myocardial stunning, stress-induced CMP and catecholamine-induced CMP. It affects middle-aged females (F >>> M), follows chronic stress/sympathetic overactivity and causes transient LV dysfunction with a hypokinetic ballooned apex (catecholamine-induced transient myocardial stunning).

units.title: Takotsubo Investigations, Angiographic and ECHO Findings, Prognosis, Short-Term Complications and Treatment
units.sec: Takotsubo Investigations, Angiographic and ECHO Findings, Prognosis, Short-Term Complications and Treatment
units.guide:
Takotsubo ECG can mimic ACS or acute HF; troponin I rises but with a reduced rate of rise, and NT-proBNP rises markedly (p345).
Angiography shows normal coronaries, a hypokinetic apex and a hypercontractile base; ECHO shows regional wall-motion abnormality not confined to one coronary territory.
Long-term prognosis is excellent. Short-term complications are shock, LV rupture and thromboembolism, bracketed as the same as MI. Treatment is no specific therapy and carvedilol.
